newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota says does not intend to curb exports to US.
newsitem.headline: Toyota says does not intend to curb exports to US.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp., Japan's top carmaker, said Friday it had no intention of curbing its car exports to the United States, despite recent concerns over recurring U.S.-Japan trade friction.

"We've set up our plans based on our supply-and-demand outlook and our U.S. exports this year will be up 5 percent year-on-year," President Hiroshi Okuda told a news conference. In calendar 1996, Toyota exported 433,000 cars to the United States.
A recent surge in Japan's car exports to the United States was a factor behind the rise in Japan's contentious trade surplus, often a source of bitter disputes between the economic giants.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto heard concerns about the surplus from both the United States and Europe at last month's summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Denver.
After the summit, President Clinton said that Japan would risk an economic war with the United States if its trade surplus started exploding again.

On Wednesday, the Finance Ministry said Japan's current account surplus jumped 155 percent in May to 907 billion yen ($7.95 billion). The surplus in merchandise trade alone surged 118.6 percent from a year earlier to 928 billion yen ($8.14 billion).

The yen's recent weakness spurred Japanese car exports by making them cheaper abroad, but Toyota played down the possibility that currency rates would spark new trade tussles between Japan and the United States.
"The current levels are unlikely to cause such problems," the Toyota chief told reporters.
The dollar was around 113.75 yen in Tokyo Friday.
